source.citation: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), Software Architecture in Practice, 4th edition.
source.scope: Tactic entries in the ten quality-attribute taxonomies in chapters 4–13. Shared decisions retain references to each applicable figure. Realizations are described within the tactic.
source.mapping: KatalIArc relates the design decisions to ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics or subcharacteristics where their effects are relevant, and preserves additional quality attributes.
source.use: Use entries as candidates. Establish applicability and evidence for the current scenario.

tactics.name: Observe conditions that indicate faults
tactics.mechanism: Check selected device or process states against expected operating conditions.
conditions: Observable conditions are tied to failure or hazard analysis.
limitations: Monitoring can consume resources and miss uninstrumented conditions.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Detect abnormal execution
tactics.mechanism: Make erroneous states observable through exceptions, deadline checks, or checks on parameters.
conditions: The execution environment exposes meaningful error signals.
limitations: Detection needs a handler or a recovery policy.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Increase restart scope when recovery fails
tactics.mechanism: Start with a small restart and broaden it when the fault persists.
conditions: Components have defined restart boundaries and preserve needed state.
limitations: A broader restart raises disruption and resource contention.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Enable independent operation across more conditions
tactics.mechanism: Give a component the state or capability to handle situations previously delegated to an external dependency.
conditions: The fallback can maintain necessary policy and consistency.
limitations: Extra local behavior can duplicate responsibility or use old information.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Continue critical functions with reduced service
tactics.mechanism: Shed or replace less important work through a planned degraded mode.
conditions: Critical functions and safe degradation boundaries are agreed.
limitations: Reduced fidelity or throughput must remain acceptable.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Handle exceptions at an appropriate boundary
tactics.mechanism: Route failures to handlers that can report, mask, repair, or contain their effects.
conditions: Error contracts identify who can handle each failure.
limitations: Masking an unhandled condition can hide a continuing failure.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Observe component health
tactics.mechanism: Have a monitor collect health signals across components and correlate deviations.
conditions: Components expose relevant health signals.
limitations: A faulty or overloaded monitor can miss symptoms.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Expect periodic liveness signals
tactics.mechanism: Have a component emit a regular signal that its monitor expects within a window.
conditions: A monitoring process and a heartbeat interval are defined.
limitations: Heartbeat traffic consumes resources and demonstrates liveness more readily than correctness.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Discard inputs identified as faulty
tactics.mechanism: Detect suspect outputs or messages and exclude them from processing.
conditions: Faulty and meaningful behavior can be distinguished.
limitations: False classification can discard valid work.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Update software during service
tactics.mechanism: Introduce a code change by patching or migrating components while other responsibilities remain available.
conditions: Old and new states or versions can operate safely through the transition.
limitations: State bridges and version compatibility add complexity.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Keep the forwarding function active during control restart
tactics.mechanism: Preserve forwarding state while a failed control element is restarted or replaced.
conditions: Forwarding can continue independently for a bounded period.
limitations: Topology or policy changes may make the preserved state stale.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Anticipate faults or hazards with a model
tactics.mechanism: Use monitored signals and a model to detect approaching unsafe or faulty states before failure.
conditions: A reliable signal and a validated threshold or model are available.
limitations: Prediction error can cause missed faults and unnecessary intervention.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Prevent faults that would surface as exceptions
tactics.mechanism: Use safeguards such as range-safe abstractions, integrity checks, or resource-safe wrappers at sensitive boundaries.
conditions: Likely error classes and the offending boundaries are known.
limitations: Controls cover the modeled errors and can add overhead.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Probe reachability
tactics.mechanism: Exchange a request and reply to check whether a peer or path is responding.
conditions: A deadline distinguishes useful replies from stale replies.
limitations: A slow path can resemble a failed peer.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Reassign responsibilities after failure
tactics.mechanism: Change the operating configuration to use working elements in place of failed ones.
conditions: A feasible configuration can preserve critical constraints.
limitations: Reconfiguration may take time and can leave state inconsistent.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Provision a standby able to take over
tactics.mechanism: Keep spare capacity and transfer responsibility to it when the active element fails.
conditions: The standby can recover the needed state and be promoted exclusively.
limitations: Shared dependencies and stale state can defeat failover.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Withdraw a component temporarily to prevent failure
tactics.mechanism: Remove an element proactively for corrective or preventive maintenance before it fails.
conditions: Other capacity can handle work and work can drain safely.
limitations: Withdrawal diminishes capacity and can interrupt work.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Bring a returning component's state up to date
tactics.mechanism: Restore or reconcile state from a current peer or recovery log before reinstatement.
conditions: An authoritative source and a consistency rule are available.
limitations: Large state transfers delay reentry.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Retry transient failures
tactics.mechanism: Reattempt an operation after a recoverable failure under a bounded retry policy.
conditions: The operation is safe to retry or effects are deduplicated.
limitations: Retries increase load and can duplicate effects.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Restore a prior acceptable state
tactics.mechanism: Recover state from an earlier checkpoint suitable for resuming work or safe operation.
conditions: An acceptable checkpoint remains available after failure.
limitations: Work after the checkpoint can be lost and external effects may need reconciliation.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Check results for plausibility
tactics.mechanism: Check values at a boundary against ranges and relationships that are feasible in context.
conditions: The valid relationships and ranges are known.
limitations: A wrong result may still appear plausible.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Have components exercise their own health checks
tactics.mechanism: Run diagnostic operations to distinguish functioning states from failure states.
conditions: Tests can exercise the intended failure modes.
limitations: Self-tests can add load and may not cover the fault.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Observe a repaired element before reinstatement
tactics.mechanism: Feed the recovered element representative inputs while withholding its authority to affect live results.
conditions: Output can be compared before authority is transferred.
limitations: The observation window cannot expose every fault.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Track timing or order of events
tactics.mechanism: Annotate events with timing or sequence information and detect unexpected delays or ordering.
conditions: The ordering and clock assumptions are explicit.
limitations: Clock skew and retransmission can produce ambiguous results.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Use transactional change boundaries
tactics.mechanism: Commit related state changes atomically with isolation appropriate to the invariant.
conditions: The data store covers the required changes and enforces the intended isolation.
limitations: External side effects or failover durability require separate guarantees.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Choose an outcome by voting across replicas
tactics.mechanism: Compare results from redundant elements and accept an outcome using a defined voting policy.
conditions: Independent results and a decision rule can be obtained.
limitations: Common-mode failures degrade the value of agreement.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §4.2, fig. 4.3 (p. 56)

tactics.name: Deliver required runtime dependencies together
tactics.mechanism: Bundle or pin the runtime dependencies expected by deployable artifacts.
conditions: The platform supports repeatable dependency packaging.
limitations: Larger artifacts and stale bundled dependencies increase maintenance.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §5.4, fig. 5.3 (p. 78)

tactics.name: Control feature activation separately from release
tactics.mechanism: Use configuration to turn deployed behavior on or off without replacing the release.
conditions: Feature boundaries and configuration ownership are defined.
limitations: Combinations of switches increase test and support effort.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §5.4, fig. 5.3 (p. 78)

tactics.name: Support interactions among coexisting versions
tactics.mechanism: Control version negotiation or compatibility so services can interact while rollout is in progress.
conditions: Contracts and compatible version ranges are known.
limitations: Supporting versions concurrently prolongs complexity.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §5.4, fig. 5.3 (p. 78)

tactics.name: Restore a previously deployed release
tactics.mechanism: Retain a working version and a means to redirect or reinstall it when the new version fails.
conditions: Persistent state and interfaces remain compatible with the rollback path.
limitations: An irreversible migration can make a release rollback unsafe.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §5.4, fig. 5.3 (p. 78)

tactics.name: Automate deployment steps
tactics.mechanism: Encode repeatable installation and deployment operations in scripts.
conditions: Deployment inputs, dependencies, and failure handling are defined.
limitations: A faulty script can repeat an error across many targets.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §5.4, fig. 5.3 (p. 78)

tactics.name: Release in controlled stages
tactics.mechanism: Roll out to a limited group first and increase coverage as observations justify it.
conditions: Traffic can be assigned to rollout groups and health can be checked.
limitations: Multiple active versions complicate support and testing.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §5.4, fig. 5.3 (p. 78)

tactics.name: Update resource energy profiles during operation
tactics.mechanism: Infer or refine energy estimates from recent telemetry and workload behavior.
conditions: Representative counters or samples can be captured.
limitations: Models can drift and instrumentation has a cost.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Estimate energy use from resource profiles
tactics.mechanism: Associate resources with documented consumption estimates for operating modes.
conditions: Resource modes and indicative power values are known.
limitations: Static estimates may miss workload-dependent variation.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Find resources with better energy characteristics
tactics.mechanism: Look up suitable execution resources using energy or cost information.
conditions: Comparable resource information and migration options are available.
limitations: Moving work can erase anticipated energy savings.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Measure energy use of resources
tactics.mechanism: Collect power or energy readings at the granularity needed for decisions.
conditions: Instrumentation and workload attribution are available.
limitations: Measurement can be costly and aggregate readings can hide individual consumers.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Shift resources into lower-energy states
tactics.mechanism: Idle, slow, or release resources when their full capability is unnecessary.
conditions: Workload constraints tolerate reduced capacity or wake-up delay.
limitations: Transitions can increase latency and affect availability.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Schedule work around energy use
tactics.mechanism: Place work at times or on resources that achieve energy goals within service limits.
conditions: Jobs can be shifted or assigned with known deadlines.
limitations: Scheduling can delay work or concentrate load.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Extract shared capabilities behind a common contract
tactics.mechanism: Move similar responsibilities behind an abstraction used by several components.
conditions: The responsibilities vary in ways the abstraction can represent.
limitations: A shared abstraction can tie callers to changes or generalize too early.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Adapt an interface to a consuming component
tactics.mechanism: Tailor the interface or translate between component contracts at a boundary.
conditions: Type, protocol, and meaning can be mapped accurately.
limitations: Translation can lose information or hide incompatible semantics.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)

tactics.name: Coordinate access to shared resources
tactics.mechanism: Mediate how participating components acquire and release common resources.
conditions: Ownership, quotas, and resource lifetimes are agreed.
limitations: Resource mediation adds overhead and can bottleneck participants.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)

tactics.name: Configure component behavior for integration
tactics.mechanism: Expose configuration points that let a component fit different collaborators.
conditions: The necessary variations are identified and supported by the contract.
limitations: Configuration variants increase combinations to validate.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)

tactics.name: Find suitable components through discovery
tactics.mechanism: Select a service or component at use time using published capabilities or registration.
conditions: Capability descriptions and discovery behavior are dependable.
limitations: Discovery adds runtime dependency and can return stale registrations.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Expose internals through explicit interfaces
tactics.mechanism: Route interactions through a contract that hides component internals.
conditions: The contract can express the interactions consumers need.
limitations: Encapsulation creates a contract boundary that must itself evolve.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Introduce an intermediary between dependent parts
tactics.mechanism: Mediate interactions so each party can depend on a stable intermediary.
conditions: The intermediary can preserve the required semantics.
limitations: The intermediary introduces cost, latency, and another dependency.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Coordinate work through an orchestration boundary
tactics.mechanism: Centralize sequencing and invocation rules for collaborating components.
conditions: The coordinator can observe the progress needed to schedule components.
limitations: Coordination adds dependencies and becomes a failure or contention point.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)

tactics.name: Constrain which components may communicate
tactics.mechanism: Permit connections only through defined paths that keep coupling manageable.
conditions: Allowed dependencies and exceptions can be identified.
limitations: Overly rigid restrictions can complicate legitimate collaborations.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)

tactics.name: Use common interface standards
tactics.mechanism: Align component interfaces, formats, and protocols with a shared specification.
conditions: Candidate parts implement compatible versions of the standard.
limitations: Conformance alone leaves domain semantics and operational behavior to verify.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §7.3, fig. 7.3 (p. 106)

tactics.name: Compose cross-cutting behavior during build
tactics.mechanism: Isolate cross-cutting responsibilities and compose them where needed at build time.
conditions: The design and toolchain can express and inspect composition points.
limitations: Implicit interception can obscure behavior and debugging.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Parameterize variation at build time
tactics.mechanism: Bind build-time options to specialize the resulting artifact.
conditions: The variation points are known before deployment.
limitations: Changing a bound value requires rebuild and redeployment.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Choose behavior at deployment or startup
tactics.mechanism: Read configuration at setup so one built artifact can operate in several environments.
conditions: Settings are validated and available when binding occurs.
limitations: Invalid combinations can fail initialization or alter behavior unexpectedly.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Dispatch through a common interface
tactics.mechanism: Bind behavior to a chosen implementation behind a stable abstraction.
conditions: Implementations honor the substitution contract.
limitations: Variant dispatch and compatibility increase complexity.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Place related responsibilities together
tactics.mechanism: Move misplaced work to the modules responsible for the same kinds of changes.
conditions: Ownership and change patterns can be identified.
limitations: Moves can change interfaces and require dependency migration.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Keep changeable resources outside executable code
tactics.mechanism: Load resources such as localization or templates from replaceable files.
conditions: Resources can be validated against a stable format.
limitations: Resources and software can drift if versioning is unmanaged.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Constrain dependency directions and scope
tactics.mechanism: Define which modules can rely on one another and enforce the constraint.
conditions: The intended module boundaries and exceptional paths are known.
limitations: Exceptions erode the restriction and tight rules can add indirection.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Interpret parameters at runtime
tactics.mechanism: Allow runtime input to select among defined behaviors.
conditions: Safe parameter ranges, privileges, and defaults are known.
limitations: Additional variability adds validation effort and runtime overhead.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Bind decisions through a shared repository
tactics.mechanism: Read changeable policies or data from a shared store during execution.
conditions: Consumers can coordinate updates and understand the data contract.
limitations: The store becomes a runtime dependency and old values may be cached.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Divide a module into cohesive units
tactics.mechanism: Split responsibilities across boundaries that group work with similar reasons to change.
conditions: Responsibilities can be separated with a manageable interface.
limitations: Poor boundaries introduce new coupling and calls.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Choose component implementations at build time
tactics.mechanism: Select an alternate component when assembling the product while preserving its contract.
conditions: Alternative components meet the stable interface and build can choose among them.
limitations: Each implementation and assembly variant needs separate verification.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §8.2, fig. 8.3 (p. 123)

tactics.name: Set limits on execution demand
tactics.mechanism: Use algorithms or work budgets with an enforceable upper bound on processing.
conditions: Work can stop or degrade safely when budget runs out.
limitations: Approximation or early termination can weaken results.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Limit queued work
tactics.mechanism: Apply a queue bound and define behavior when available slots are exhausted.
conditions: The allowed queue length and overload policy are known.
limitations: The system must delay, shed, or reject work when full.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)

tactics.name: Overlap or parallelize work
tactics.mechanism: Run independent work concurrently to reduce time spent waiting for resources.
conditions: The work can be divided safely and synchronization is defined.
limitations: Coordination and contention can eliminate the expected gain.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)

tactics.name: Regulate incoming work
tactics.mechanism: Control incoming request rates or sample streams at a rate the system can sustain.
conditions: Arrival or sampling can be governed and fidelity requirements are known.
limitations: Dropped samples or constrained requests can reduce utility.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Keep additional copies near readers
tactics.mechanism: Cache or replicate data to relieve contention or avoid slow access paths.
conditions: Staleness and update rules suit read requirements.
limitations: Copies require space and can return inconsistent or outdated data.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)

tactics.name: Choose more efficient computation
tactics.mechanism: Select algorithms or representations that reduce the work required for an equivalent response.
conditions: The chosen approach suits the workload sizes and distributions.
limitations: A local efficiency gain can shift work or storage elsewhere.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Provision more processing or storage capacity
tactics.mechanism: Increase the available amount of the resource that constrains delivery.
conditions: Measurement identifies a resource bottleneck that can be expanded.
limitations: Shared bottlenecks and cost can limit the gain.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)

tactics.name: Cap how much event work is serviced
tactics.mechanism: Limit acceptance or processing when demand would exceed a service budget.
conditions: Queuing and overflow behavior are defined.
limitations: Some events wait longer or are dropped.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Prefer time-critical events
tactics.mechanism: Schedule work by importance and defer optional work when demand is excessive.
conditions: Priorities reflect scenario requirements and overload behavior is agreed.
limitations: Low-priority work can starve.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Remove work from the common path
tactics.mechanism: Reduce repeated transformations, interactions, or mediation needed to process each event.
conditions: Tracing or analysis identifies avoidable work.
limitations: Removing a boundary can increase coupling or reduce flexibility.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)
Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §6.2, fig. 6.3 (p. 93)

tactics.name: Use multiple instances of a computation
tactics.mechanism: Distribute work across instances placed where it can be processed more efficiently.
conditions: Work is routable and the state strategy allows multiple instances.
limitations: Routing and state consistency can become bottlenecks.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)

tactics.name: Schedule access to constrained resources
tactics.mechanism: Choose an assignment order and sharing policy for work requesting scarce resources.
conditions: Demand, deadlines, and allocation rules are measurable.
limitations: Unfair scheduling or preemption overhead can harm some workloads.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §9.2, fig. 9.3 (p. 144)

tactics.name: Terminate an operation before it causes harm
tactics.mechanism: Interrupt hazardous work when a safety condition is violated.
conditions: Termination itself can leave the system safe.
limitations: Effects already committed may require a recovery step.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Detect unsafe divergences between synchronized outputs
tactics.mechanism: Compare redundant outputs to detect a mismatch before depending on them.
conditions: The outputs are comparable and available within the required time.
limitations: Shared faults may produce identical unsafe outputs.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Detect hazardous timing omissions
tactics.mechanism: Treat missed deadlines as indications that an operation may have failed or become unsafe.
conditions: Timing bounds reflect the hazard analysis.
limitations: Variable delays can cause false detections.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Use separate ways to determine a safe result
tactics.mechanism: Combine independent requirements, inputs, or calculations for the safety-relevant outcome.
conditions: Comparing unlike signals can be done within the required assurance and time.
limitations: Reconciliation is more complex and inputs may share dependencies.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Provide independent implementations of a function
tactics.mechanism: Use design diversity to reduce shared implementation faults across components.
conditions: Independent implementations can satisfy the same functional contract.
limitations: Specification errors can cause correlated failure.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Enforce safe operation sequences
tactics.mechanism: Gate access to a protected operation until the required events and preconditions hold.
conditions: The interlock can observe and control every relevant entry path.
limitations: Incomplete observation or a failed interlock can block or admit work incorrectly.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Place barriers between hazard domains
tactics.mechanism: Separate components or propagation paths to contain the effects of unsafe behavior.
conditions: The barrier covers the identified channels through which hazards can spread.
limitations: Shared dependencies may still propagate an effect.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Mask an unsafe output through redundancy
tactics.mechanism: Use redundant outputs and a selection rule to prevent one faulty output from reaching consumers.
conditions: Enough independently correct outputs remain for the policy to work.
limitations: A faulty voter or common cause can pass a dangerous output.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Repair the fields needed for safe operation
tactics.mechanism: Identify damaged state and rebuild or correct it to reach a safe configuration.
conditions: An authoritative source and conditions for safe continuation are known.
limitations: Partial repair may preserve inconsistencies or lose detail.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Provide identical redundant components
tactics.mechanism: Use replicas to retain critical behavior when an individual component fails.
conditions: Random failures are sufficiently independent and failure detection is adequate.
limitations: Identical implementations share design defects.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Use a simpler independent protection mechanism
tactics.mechanism: Move a protective function to an independent or more predictable component where feasible.
conditions: The protected operation and assurance need can be isolated.
limitations: The substitute still depends on its own interface and failure assumptions.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §10.2, fig. 10.3 (p. 157)

tactics.name: Record activity for incident investigation
tactics.mechanism: Record attributable security events so activity can be reconstructed later.
conditions: Identity, event provenance, and protected log storage are available.
limitations: Audit data can be incomplete, costly, or sensitive.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Verify claimed identity
tactics.mechanism: Require suitable proof of identity before creating an authenticated session or accepting a request.
conditions: A trusted identity mechanism and recovery process are available.
limitations: Compromised credentials or identity providers can defeat verification.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Check permission for a requested action
tactics.mechanism: Evaluate the verified actor's permission to act on the specified resource.
conditions: The policy distinguishes actors, resources, and operations.
limitations: An incomplete policy or bypass path can admit unauthorized actions.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Replace weak or exposed credential settings
tactics.mechanism: Change default or compromised credential settings and support safe updates.
conditions: Credential ownership and update procedures are known.
limitations: Changing credentials can affect dependent clients or lock out valid users.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Detect suspicious timing in message delivery
tactics.mechanism: Flag timing anomalies that may signal interference in message delivery.
conditions: Expected delay distributions are known.
limitations: Congestion or clock drift can also introduce anomalies.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Detect suspicious loss of service capacity
tactics.mechanism: Monitor abnormal load or loss of availability to identify possible intentional resource exhaustion.
conditions: Normal load and response thresholds are known.
limitations: Demand surges may resemble attacks.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Detect patterns of unauthorized behavior
tactics.mechanism: Compare observed activity with security signals and raise alarms for suspicious patterns.
conditions: Relevant telemetry and response ownership are available.
limitations: Signatures miss some attacks and can produce false positives.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Make sensitive data unreadable without authorized keys
tactics.mechanism: Encrypt selected data at the boundaries required by the threat model and control access to keys.
conditions: Key generation, distribution, storage, and rotation are defined.
limitations: Compromised endpoints or keys can reveal data and encryption can add overhead.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Bind requests to actor identifiers
tactics.mechanism: Associate actors or components with distinct identities for later security decisions.
conditions: Identifiers can be issued and managed consistently.
limitations: An identifier presented by a requester still needs verification.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Notify affected parties about a security incident
tactics.mechanism: Send incident information to parties that can respond within an agreed workflow.
conditions: The system can route notices to authorized recipients.
limitations: Late or noisy notices delay effective response.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Constrain access to protected resources
tactics.mechanism: Restrict paths or privileges through which actors can reach sensitive resources.
conditions: All relevant access paths can be enforced consistently.
limitations: Restrictions carry operational complexity and can be circumvented via uncontrolled paths.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Reduce reachable attack surfaces and damage paths
tactics.mechanism: Limit which operations or data are exposed and bound the reach of each exposed interface.
conditions: The threat model identifies exposure paths and required access.
limitations: Exposure limits can reduce usability or flexibility.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Retain verifiable evidence of an action
tactics.mechanism: Bind an action to its actor and preserve verifiable evidence of what occurred.
conditions: Identity binding, time assumptions, and evidence retention are trustworthy.
limitations: Compromised keys or missing evidence can undermine attribution.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Limit access attempts after suspicious activity
tactics.mechanism: Throttle or temporarily restrict authentication attempts under a policy.
conditions: Attempt tracking and recovery channels are available.
limitations: Limits can block legitimate users or be exploited to trigger lockout.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Withdraw affected grants or sessions
tactics.mechanism: Disable permissions, sessions, or credentials associated with a detected incident.
conditions: The system can invalidate delegated or cached authority.
limitations: Revocation can be delayed or disrupt legitimate work.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Isolate different trust domains
tactics.mechanism: Separate data, privileges, or workloads so a compromise in one domain has limited reach.
conditions: Boundaries and cross-domain exchanges are enforceable.
limitations: Isolation is harder with shared privileges or uncontrolled dependencies.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Accept only input that satisfies declared constraints
tactics.mechanism: Check input at trust boundaries against expected types, formats, and semantic rules.
conditions: The receiving boundary knows the valid input contract.
limitations: Incomplete checks leave unmodeled cases and validation adds work.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Check integrity of received data
tactics.mechanism: Verify protected digests or authentication information before using data.
conditions: The expected check value or key is obtained through a trusted channel.
limitations: A checksum alone detects corruption rather than proving an origin.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §11.2, fig. 11.3 (p. 173)

tactics.name: Allow tests to substitute data sources
tactics.mechanism: Access data through contracts that can be supplied by controlled test implementations.
conditions: Test substitutes model the features required by the scenario.
limitations: Differences between test and production data paths can conceal failures.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Check invariants during test execution
tactics.mechanism: Run assertions that report violated expectations close to the responsible operation.
conditions: Expected invariants and useful diagnostics are defined.
limitations: Assertions can be costly or omit failures outside their scope.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Make test-relevant behavior reproducible
tactics.mechanism: Control variability such as time, scheduling, and external responses in tests.
conditions: Sources of variability are identifiable and configurable.
limitations: Artificial determinism can hide defects that occur under real scheduling.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Reduce the structural states a test must cover
tactics.mechanism: Limit unnecessary control flow and interactions so tests can exercise meaningful combinations.
conditions: The design identifies complexity that adds no required behavior.
limitations: Simplification may move complexity across an interface.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Keep test-relevant state in accessible locations
tactics.mechanism: Concentrate state or expose stable access so tests can establish and inspect it.
conditions: The design identifies state that determines the expected behavior.
limitations: Concentration can reduce isolation or increase contention.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Replay recorded interactions
tactics.mechanism: Capture enough events or inputs to reproduce a prior execution in a test.
conditions: Relevant external effects and timing can be reproduced or simulated.
limitations: Captures may omit sources of nondeterminism and can contain sensitive data.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Contain experiments in a test environment
tactics.mechanism: Run selected elements in a controlled environment with bounded external effects.
conditions: Dependencies can be simulated or isolated safe substitutes are available.
limitations: A sandbox may differ from the deployed environment.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Expose controlled interfaces for testing
tactics.mechanism: Provide a controlled way for tests to set inputs or inspect internal state.
conditions: Test access can be isolated or restricted and states have clear meaning.
limitations: Test interfaces can create maintenance effort and security exposure.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §12.2, fig. 12.4 (p. 191)

tactics.name: Let users act on a group
tactics.mechanism: Support applying an operation to a selected set of related objects.
conditions: Bulk effects and partial failure behavior are explicit.
limitations: A mistaken bulk action can affect more items.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §13.2, fig. 13.3 (p. 202)

tactics.name: Allow users to cancel ongoing work
tactics.mechanism: Provide a means to interrupt an operation and recover control at a safe point.
conditions: An operation can be interrupted or compensated safely.
limitations: Some external effects cannot be cancelled immediately.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §13.2, fig. 13.3 (p. 202)

tactics.name: Let a user interrupt and resume work
tactics.mechanism: Save progress and restore the operation after a user-requested pause.
conditions: The operation has safe pause points and revivable state.
limitations: Paused work can retain resources or expire.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §13.2, fig. 13.3 (p. 202)

tactics.name: Represent internal progress for feedback
tactics.mechanism: Track runtime state so the product can explain what it is doing and what to expect.
conditions: Progress and meaningful states are observable.
limitations: Estimates can mislead when operations are variable.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §13.2, fig. 13.3 (p. 202)

tactics.name: Represent the user's task and progress
tactics.mechanism: Represent known workflows so the system can present guidance suitable to the active task.
conditions: Common tasks and their states are modeled.
limitations: Rigid workflows can frustrate unanticipated task paths.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §13.2, fig. 13.3 (p. 202)

tactics.name: Allow users to reverse eligible actions
tactics.mechanism: Retain enough state or information to reverse supported operations.
conditions: Reversibility and history bounds are agreed.
limitations: Irreversible external effects require a different recovery path.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §13.2, fig. 13.3 (p. 202)

tactics.name: Adapt interaction to user preferences or skills
tactics.mechanism: Maintain relevant preferences or inferred skill so the interaction can be tailored.
conditions: Available signals and permitted use of user information are established.
limitations: Inaccurate models can surface unsuitable behavior.
source_refs: Bass, Clements, and Kazman (2021), 4th ed., §13.2, fig. 13.3 (p. 202)
